title: Talbot, Negatives and the Race of 1839
summary: An English gentleman who could not draw found a way to let sunlight draw for him on paper. His trick was a backwards picture called a negative, which could print copy after copy. Meanwhile, inventors in France and Brazil were racing to the same idea.

sections.heading: A Bad Artist on a Beautiful Lake
paragraphs: Picture a sunny October day in 1833 on the shores of Lake Como in northern Italy. Mountains rise straight out of blue water, villas glow pink and yellow along the edge, and a 33-year-old Englishman is sitting with a sketchbook, getting more and more annoyed. His name is William Henry Fox Talbot, and he is trying to draw the view. He is failing.

Talbot was not lazy, and he was certainly not stupid. Born on 11 February 1800 at Melbury House in Dorset, he had studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, finishing in 1821 among the top mathematics students of his year. He wrote papers on light, coloured flames and mathematics, and in 1831 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, Britain's most famous club of scientists. His family home was Lacock Abbey in Wiltshire, a rambling stone house that had begun life in 1232 as a nunnery. He could read ancient languages, study plants and do hard sums. What he could not do was draw.

To help, he was using a camera lucida, the drawing aid you met in Part 2. It is a small glass prism on a stick. When you look down through it, you seem to see the scene and your paper at the same time, as if the view were floating on the page, so you can trace it. In theory, anyone can then draw like a professional. In practice, the moment Talbot moved his eye, the ghostly image slid around, and when he took his eye away he found, as he later wrote, only a few sad, wandering pencil lines on the paper.

He remembered that years before he had tried the older trick, the camera obscura, which throws a bright image onto paper inside a box. That had not gone well either. But the memory of those lovely little pictures sitting on the paper set him thinking. Talbot later described the moment in his own words in a short history he published in 1844. He was, he said, "amusing myself on the lovely shores of the Lake of Como, in Italy" when an idea struck him: what if the natural images of the camera could be made to print themselves on paper and stay there?

It was the same dream Thomas Wedgwood and Humphry Davy had chased in 1802, and the same one Niépce and Daguerre were quietly working on in France. Talbot did not know how far the French had got. He only knew that light changes silver, and that he was a good enough chemist to find out how.

sections.heading: Photogenic Drawing: Salt, Silver and Sunlight
paragraphs: Talbot returned to England in January 1834 and began experimenting at Lacock. His recipe sounds almost like cooking. First he soaked a sheet of good writing paper in a weak solution of ordinary table salt, which is sodium chloride, and let it dry. Then he brushed one side with silver nitrate dissolved in water. Where the two chemicals met inside the fibres of the paper, they made silver chloride, a light-sensitive silver halide. (Remember the glossary word: a silver halide is silver joined to chlorine, bromine or iodine.)

Now he laid things on top of the paper: a leaf, a feather, a piece of lace, and pressed them flat under glass. He set the sandwich out in the sun. Over minutes, the uncovered paper darkened to a deep purple-brown, while the paper under the leaf stayed pale. When he lifted the leaf off, there was its outline in white, every vein showing, on a dark background. These were contact prints, made by touching an object to the paper, and Talbot later called the whole technique photogenic drawing, which means a drawing produced by light.

He made a surprising discovery along the way. You might guess that more salt would make the paper more sensitive. Instead he found the opposite. As he put it, "a lesser quantity of salt produced a greater effect." The trick was to leave a little extra silver nitrate in the paper compared with the salt. By brushing on more silver, drying, and brushing again, he made paper sensitive enough to catch the dim image inside a camera.

That still left the old problem from Part 2. Unused silver salt in the white parts of a picture would keep darkening whenever it saw daylight, until everything turned the same dull colour. Talbot found a partial fix. He soaked finished pictures in a strong solution of salt, or in potassium iodide, which made the leftover silver much less sensitive. He called this stabilizing rather than truly fixing. It worked well enough that some of his 1830s pictures still survive, though many have faded and yellowed.

Camera pictures were much harder than contact prints. Inside a camera, the light reaching the paper is weak, and in 1834 Talbot's exposures of buildings were too faint to show detail. So he built small wooden cameras with short lenses, which made tiny but brighter images, and he scattered several around the grounds at Lacock to work at once. With paper given repeated washes of salt and silver, he wrote, a bright day could produce a picture in about ten minutes.

sections.heading: The Window Smaller Than a Stamp
paragraphs: In August 1835, Talbot pointed one of his little cameras at a tall window in the south gallery of Lacock Abbey. It is an oriel window, a kind of bay window that sticks out from the wall, divided by stone bars and filled with a lattice of small diamond-shaped glass panes. Bright daylight came through the glass and the dark stone frame stood out sharply against it. That strong contrast made it perfect for a slow, weak process.

The result is now the oldest known surviving camera negative in the world. It is astonishingly small. The image itself measures only about 35 by 29 millimetres, roughly the size of a large postage stamp. Look closely and you can see the stone bars of the window and the crisscross pattern of the panes. But something is strange about it: the window glass, which was the brightest thing in the scene, looks dark, and the shadowy stone looks pale.

That is what a negative is. Light darkened the silver, so the brightest parts of the scene became the darkest parts of the picture. A bright sky turns black and a dark coat turns white. At first this seems like a failure. Talbot realised it was actually a gift. If you put a negative on top of a fresh sheet of sensitive paper and shine light through it, the dark parts of the negative block the light and the pale parts let it through. The new print comes out reversed a second time, which means the right way round. And because the negative itself does not get used up, you can do it again and again.

This idea, which later historians call the negative-positive process, is the most important thing in this part. It is how almost all film photography worked for about 150 years. Every school photo printed on paper from film, every holiday snapshot handed out in envelopes in the 1980s, comes from this little stamp-sized window.

The famous negative is now in the collection of the Science Museum Group in Britain and is cared for at the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford. It is kept mostly in the dark, because even today light can damage it. Lacock Abbey itself belongs to the National Trust, and the Fox Talbot Museum there tells his story. Harry Potter fans may recognise the cloisters of Lacock, too: scenes from several of the films were shot there.

Then Talbot did something that, in hindsight, seems almost unbelievable. He put photography aside. He was busy with mathematics, optics, plants and the running of a large country estate, and he seems to have felt there was no hurry. He did not publish anything about his pictures. For more than three years, the oldest camera negative in the world sat quietly among his papers.

sections.heading: January 1839: The Race Begins
paragraphs: On 7 January 1839, as you saw in Part 4, François Arago stood up at the French Academy of Sciences in Paris and announced that Louis Daguerre had found a way to fix the images of the camera. Arago did not explain how the process worked; he only described the astonishing results. Within days the news was in newspapers across Europe.

Imagine Talbot reading it at Lacock. He had been making camera pictures since 1835, and now a Frenchman was about to get all the credit. Worse, he could not tell from the reports whether Daguerre's method was the same as his. If it was, the world might think Talbot had copied it. He moved fast.

On 25 January 1839, less than three weeks after Arago's speech, some of Talbot's photogenic drawings went on show at the Royal Institution in London, the famous science hall where the great experimenter Michael Faraday gave lectures. Within about a fortnight, Talbot sent a paper to the Royal Society explaining his work, and a few weeks later he gave the full details of how to make sensitive paper and how to stabilize the images. Unlike Daguerre, who was still keeping his recipe secret while the French government decided how to reward him, Talbot told everyone exactly what he did.

Then the two methods were finally compared, and they turned out to be completely different. Daguerre's picture was a single, mirror-like image on a polished silver plate. Talbot's was a negative on paper. Daguerre's was far sharper and more detailed; people gasped at the tiny letters you could read on signs with a magnifying glass. Talbot's paper images were soft and fuzzy, because the light spread out through the fibres of the paper. But Talbot's could be copied.

There was one more twist in the race. France gave Daguerre's process to the world free on 19 August 1839. But a few days earlier, Daguerre's agent had taken out a patent on it in England and Wales. So the free gift was not quite free everywhere: in England, you were supposed to pay for a licence to make daguerreotypes. Patents, as we will see, became a big part of Talbot's story too.

sections.heading: Sir John Herschel: The Fixer and the Word-Maker
paragraphs: Talbot's most helpful friend in all this was Sir John Herschel, one of the most famous scientists in Britain. Herschel was an astronomer, the son of William Herschel who had discovered the planet Uranus. From 1834 to 1838 he had lived at Feldhausen near Cape Town in southern Africa, mapping the stars of the southern sky with a telescope about 21 feet long. He was back in England, full of energy, just as the photography news broke.

Herschel had an important secret weapon, though he had not realised it was a weapon. Twenty years earlier, in 1819, he had studied a chemical then called hyposulphite of soda, and found that it dissolves silver salts that water cannot touch. Today chemists call it sodium thiosulfate, but photographers still call it hypo for short.

When Herschel heard about the new pictures in early 1839, he started experimenting himself within days. He quickly saw that hypo was exactly the answer to the fixing problem. Wash a finished picture in hypo, and it dissolves away all the unused silver salt, the silver that light has not touched yet. With nothing sensitive left in the white areas, the picture can sit in sunlight without darkening. Herschel generously told both Talbot and Daguerre. Talbot was using hypo for most of his prints by the early 1840s, and Daguerre's process adopted it as well. Hypo, or its close cousin ammonium thiosulfate, is still the standard fixer in darkrooms today, nearly two centuries later.

Herschel also gave the new art its name. Talbot said photogenic drawing; Daguerre said daguerreotype. In 1839 Herschel began using the word photography, from Greek words meaning light and writing, and he was the first to use the words negative and positive for the two kinds of photographic image. He talked about them in papers read to the Royal Society in March 1839 and January 1840. These words were so useful that they spread across the world. Every time you say photo, you are using a word Herschel helped make popular.

Herschel kept inventing. On 9 September 1839 he made an image on glass of the wooden frame of his father's giant 40-foot telescope, one of the earliest photographs on glass. In 1842 he invented the cyanotype, a completely different kind of photograph that uses iron instead of silver. Paper is coated with two iron chemicals, ferric ammonium citrate and potassium ferricyanide. Where sunlight hits, they react to form Prussian blue, the same deep blue used in paints. You simply wash the paper in plain water, and the unexposed chemicals rinse away, leaving a white picture on a brilliant blue background. The cyanotype later became the blueprint, used for copying engineering and architects' drawings until about the 1940s. That is why we still call a detailed plan a blueprint.

sections.heading: Forgotten Rivals: Bayard in Paris, Florence in Brazil
paragraphs: The race of 1839 had more than two runners. In Paris, a quiet civil servant named Hippolyte Bayard, who worked at the Ministry of Finance, had been experimenting on his own. By March 1839 he had invented a way to make a positive picture directly on paper, inside the camera, with no negative needed. His pictures were soft and gentle, like Talbot's, but each one came out the right way round.

In the summer of 1839, Bayard put about thirty of his photographs on display at a charity exhibition in Paris. Many history books give the date as 24 June 1839 and call it the world's first public exhibition of photographs, though some French sources say the show actually opened in July. Either way, Bayard was showing real photographs on paper to the public before the full daguerreotype method had been revealed.

Here is where his luck ran out. François Arago, the powerful scientist who was promoting Daguerre, persuaded Bayard to wait before announcing his process. Arago was Daguerre's friend and wanted the daguerreotype to be France's great invention. The government gave Bayard 600 francs to buy better equipment. Daguerre and Isidore Niépce, by comparison, received lifetime pensions totalling 10,000 francs a year. When Bayard finally described his method to the Academy of Sciences in February 1840, the world was already talking about daguerreotypes.

Bayard answered with one of the cleverest protests in history. In October 1840 he made a photograph of himself slumped against a wall, eyes closed, shirtless, with a cloth over his lap, posed as if he were a drowned body. On the back he wrote a mocking note, pretending to be someone describing the corpse. It said, roughly, that this was the inventor Bayard, who had drowned himself in despair because the government had given so much to Daguerre and nothing to him. Of course, Bayard was perfectly alive and took the photo himself. Self Portrait as a Drowned Man is now often called the first staged or faked photograph, a reminder, as Part 17 will show, that photographs could tell stories that were not true almost from the very beginning. Bayard went on to help found the French Photographic Society and to photograph historic French buildings for a government survey in 1851.

Meanwhile, thousands of kilometres away in Brazil, another forgotten inventor had been at work even earlier. Hercules Florence was born in Nice in 1804, sailed to Rio de Janeiro in 1824, and worked as an artist on a Russian-sponsored scientific expedition into the Amazon from 1826 to 1829. He settled in the small town of Campinas, where he invented his own printing method, which he called polygraphia. Wanting a cheap way to print labels and documents, he began experimenting with silver nitrate on paper around 1832 or 1833, with help from a local pharmacist, Joaquim Corrêa de Mello.

Florence's notes use a word meaning photography, photographia or photographie, in the early 1830s, years before Herschel made the word famous. He could not fully fix his images, and when news of the daguerreotype reached Brazil in 1839 he gave up the project. Because he lived far from Europe's scientific societies and published little, almost nobody knew about him until historians, especially the Brazilian scholar Boris Kossoy, rediscovered his notebooks in the 1970s. Today a Brazilian institute, the Instituto Moreira Salles, holds an 1833 image by Florence that it describes as the oldest photographic record in the Americas. Florence, by the way, also invented a way to write down animal sounds as music, and he had 20 children.

sections.heading: The Calotype: A Beautiful Picture in a Minute
paragraphs: Talbot's paper pictures had one big weakness: they were slow. In the camera, photogenic drawing paper needed an hour or more in bright light, because the silver had to darken all by itself until the picture was visible. Daguerre had already solved that problem with the latent image, an invisible picture that a developer brings out. On 23 September 1840, Talbot found his own way to do the same thing on paper.

His new paper was coated with silver iodide. Just before use, he brushed it with a mixture he called gallo-nitrate of silver, made with gallic acid, a chemical that comes from oak galls (the round growths wasps cause on oak trees), plus silver nitrate. After a short exposure, the paper looked completely blank. But when he brushed on more gallo-nitrate and warmed the paper gently, a picture slowly bloomed out of nothing, like invisible ink appearing over a candle. The light had left a hidden mark, and the chemistry made it visible.

Instead of an hour, an exposure in bright sunshine now took about a minute or two. That was short enough for portraits, as long as the sitters were patient. Talbot named the process the calotype, from the Greek word kalos, meaning beautiful. Some people called it the talbotype in his honour.

The paper negative was then fixed, often waxed to make it more see-through, and laid on salted paper in the sun to print as many positive copies as anyone wanted. The prints were usually warm brown or reddish. Because the light passed through paper fibres twice, once in the negative and once in printing, calotypes had a soft, slightly grainy look, more like a charcoal drawing than a mirror. Artists loved that. People who wanted crisp detail preferred daguerreotypes.

Talbot patented the calotype in England in February 1841. If you wanted to use it, you needed a licence. Licences were expensive: one historian notes that Talbot took about 30 percent of a licensed studio's takings. In August 1841 Henry Collen became the first licensed professional calotype photographer.

English patents did not apply in Scotland, and there the calotype flourished. In Edinburgh, the painter David Octavius Hill and the young photographer Robert Adamson made around 3,000 photographs from calotype negatives between 1843 and 1848, including fishing families, churchmen and city scenes. In 1845 they photographed Peter Jones, also called Kahkewaquonaby, an Ojibwe minister visiting Scotland. That calotype is one of the oldest surviving photographs of a Native North American person. Their work showed that the soft paper picture could be real art.

sections.heading: Seaweed in Blue and the Pencil of Nature
paragraphs: One of the first people to see what photography could do for science was a woman named Anna Atkins. Born in Tonbridge, Kent, in 1799, she lost her mother as a baby and grew up close to her father, John George Children, a chemist and natural scientist at the British Museum. Both her father and her husband were friends of Talbot, so Atkins heard about photography almost as soon as it existed. She was also a skilled botanist who collected seaweeds and other algae.

Drawing seaweed accurately is maddening. The fronds are lacy, wavy and branching in every direction. Atkins realised that Herschel's brand-new cyanotype could do the job perfectly. She laid each dried specimen directly on cyanotype paper, set it in the sun, then rinsed the sheet in water. Out came a white silhouette of the seaweed, every delicate branch in place, floating on deep blue like an underwater ghost.

In October 1843 she published the first part of Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions. Even the text pages were made the same way, from her own handwriting printed as cyanotypes. It is often called the first book illustrated with photographs. Atkins kept adding parts for about ten years, and complete copies hold hundreds of plates; the Royal Society's copy has 389, and one at the Horniman Museum in London has 443. Only 17 copies are known to survive, so they are fantastically valuable: one sold at auction in 2004 for 229,250 pounds. Later, with her friend Anne Dixon, she made more cyanotype albums, including one of ferns in 1853.

Talbot, meanwhile, wanted to show the world what his negatives could do. In 1844 he began publishing The Pencil of Nature, the title meaning that light itself was doing the drawing. It came out in six parts between 1844 and 1846, with 24 real photographic prints pasted in by hand, and it is usually called the first commercially published book illustrated with photographs. (Atkins's book came first but was privately made for friends and scientists, not sold in shops.) Each plate came with a short essay explaining what photography might be good for: copying old documents, recording the china on your shelves in case a thief stole it, preserving buildings, or making art. The Open Door shows a broom leaning in a sunlit stone doorway, and The Haystack shows a ladder against a huge stack of hay; both look almost like paintings.

To print so many photographs, Talbot's assistant set up a workshop in Reading in 1844, sometimes called the Reading Establishment, where rows of printing frames sat out in the sun. It was a bold idea, a photograph factory, but it lost money. Many prints from the period faded, because the chemistry of fixing and washing was still poorly understood. The Pencil of Nature did not sell well either, and Talbot stopped after six parts, although he had planned more. About 40 nearly complete copies survive.

Talbot's patents also slowed things down. Many photographers felt he was trying to control the whole art, and in 1854 he took a photographer named Martin Laroche to court. The jury agreed Talbot's patent was valid, but decided that Laroche, who used the newer glass-plate method you will meet in Part 7, was not breaking it. Talbot did not renew his patent after that. By then the race had a clear winner, and in a surprising way, it was both inventors. Daguerreotypes were sharper and dominated the 1840s, but they were one of a kind. Talbot's idea of a negative that could make endless copies won in the long run, and it ruled photography until the age of digital cameras.

Yet nobody in 1850 could fully explain what was actually going on inside the silver. How does a beam of light leave an invisible mark? Why does a lens make a sharper picture than a pinhole? What does a developer really do? To find out, the next part opens up the camera and looks inside.

deepDive:
Who invented photography? Historians today mostly refuse to name one person, and the race of 1839 shows why. Niépce made the oldest surviving camera photograph around 1826 to 1827. Talbot made camera negatives by 1835. Florence was writing about his own experiments in Brazil around 1833 to 1834. Bayard made direct positives by early 1839. Daguerre's process was the first to be announced to the world and the first to become a practical, widely used method. Each person solved a different part of the problem, and several worked without knowing about the others. This pattern, called multiple or simultaneous invention, happens often in the history of technology, because many people are building on the same earlier discoveries, in this case Schulze's work on silver salts and centuries of camera obscura experience.

The chemistry of the calotype is also worth a closer look. Talbot's photogenic drawing was a printing-out process: the light itself had to make enough metallic silver to see, which needs a lot of light. The calotype was a developing-out process: the light only had to make a tiny invisible change, and the gallic acid developer did the rest, multiplying the effect enormously. That is why exposures fell from about an hour to a minute or two. Every film camera of the next 150 years used developing-out, not printing-out.

There is a real debate about Talbot's patents. Some historians argue that his licence fees and lawsuits slowed the spread of photography in England in the 1840s and early 1850s, pointing out that the calotype flourished in Scotland and France, where his English patent did not apply. Others note that Talbot spent a great deal of his own money on research and on The Pencil of Nature, and that patents were normal for inventors of his day. Daguerre, by contrast, was paid a state pension, so he could afford to let France give his process away, except in England, where his agent took out a patent.

Finally, words matter. Herschel's terms photography, negative and positive were so clear that they replaced everyone's own inventions, which is one reason he is sometimes called a hidden founder of photography even though he never claimed to have invented it.
funFact: Anna Atkins made even the text pages of her famous seaweed book as cyanotypes of her own handwriting, so the whole book, words and pictures, was printed by sunlight.

check.q: What was the big advantage of Talbot's paper negatives over Daguerre's plates?
check.a: Many positive prints could be made from one negative
wrong: They needed no light at all to make
